title: Maghrib, the sunset prayer
tomorrow: it's midnight, the phone is glowing, and 'Isha was hours ago. now?

segments.voice: 'Asr, the prayer that sits in the afternoon slide. Guard the middle prayer. Now the sun goes down, and someone has set the table.
screen: `GUARD THE MIDDLE PRAYER.` → `THE TABLE IS SET.`

segments.voice: A dinner invitation for "around sunset" sounds simple until you pray. Amira is at Jordan's grandmother's house. The roast comes out of the oven just as the sky turns orange, which is exactly when Maghrib comes in. Before anyone eats, Jordan's grandmother opens her worn Bible and reads one line from the Psalms, the way she does every evening. Amira hears it and stops: "Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray." So, the question for today: why do people mark sunset with prayer at all?
screen: `DINNER "AROUND SUNSET".` → `THE ROAST, THE ORANGE SKY.` → `EVENING, AND MORNING, AND AT NOON.`

segments.voice: Islam's answer starts with the turn of the day. The Qur'an, in Pickthall's words: "So glory be to Allah when ye enter the night and when ye enter the morning." Sunset is a door, and Maghrib is the prayer at the door. Its window opens as the sun disappears and is short, so in a report in Abu Dawud the Prophet ﷺ warns against putting it off until the stars come out. And here's the detail for Amira's dinner: in Sahih al-Bukhari, he says that when supper is served as the prayer begins, start with the supper, and don't rush. A hungry, distracted prayer isn't the goal. Now the neighbor. That line Jordan's grandmother read is Psalm fifty-five, in the King James Bible, and it goes on: "and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice." Another psalm calls prayer "the evening sacrifice." Christians who keep evening prayer, some at a church service, some at a kitchen table, are standing at the same door as the light goes. Here's the honest difference. For Muslims, Maghrib is required, with a set time, set movements, and words in Arabic. For Christians, evening prayer is a practice some keep and others don't, in their own words and language. Same door, two different ways through it. Neither one needs the other to be the same.
screen: `WHEN YE ENTER THE NIGHT.` · `SHORT WINDOW. SUPPER FIRST.` · `PSALM 55: EVENING, MORNING, NOON.` · `SAME DOOR, DIFFERENT WAYS.` · then, large: `AT SUNSET.`

segments.voice: Find the nearest window, or think back to the last sky you saw. Look at its color for the whole sit, whatever it is right now: blue, gray, orange, black. Notice that this same light is falling on a mosque, a church, a kitchen table, and on you.
screen: `THE NEAREST WINDOW.` · `JUST THE COLOR.` · `THE SAME LIGHT, EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Maghrib: the place or time of the sun's setting, and the prayer said there, in the short window as the light goes.
For tonight's sky: at sunset, a door, with more than one family standing at it. Four posts down, one to go.

howItsDone: Maghrib is prayed just after sunset in a short window; when the meal and the prayer arrive together, families either pray first or eat first and then pray, following the hadith of supper. Some Christians keep evening prayer too, at church or at home, often with a psalm.
